Meta.description: Linlin’s space for Vietnamese, English, Chinese, and Thai — blogs, short lessons, and a slow, clear way to learn.

Hero.title: Study with Linlin
Hero.subtitle: Linlin built a clear, warm corner to learn: blogs to understand, short lessons to practice, and a slow pace so it actually stays. For beginners and for anyone starting over.

About.title: I’m Linlin
About.lead: Language learning does not have to rush. It needs to be steady, clear, and a little joyful each day.
About.bio1: Linlin lives and works in Vietnam. She loves languages because they open a way of seeing daily life: a greeting, a habit, a way of telling a story. Vietnamese is home. She has studied Chinese and taught it. English and Thai are two paths she is learning now — written slowly and clearly, so others can walk with her.
About.bio2: This site is where she writes about how to study, and where short lessons will live — long enough to sit down and finish, short enough not to exhaust you. No exams. No ranking. Just a slow, readable path.
About.quote: Go a little slower, and remember it for life.

Method.title: Three steps, repeated daily
Method.subtitle: You do not need to study more. You need a small habit you can keep.
Method.step1Body: Start with the language you need most. The site follows the language you choose.
Method.step2Body: The blogs explain why a method works — memory, pacing, and common mistakes.
Method.step3Body: Lessons stay small: words, sentence patterns, listening. Then stop. Come back tomorrow.

Rhythm.title: One day, four small sessions
Rhythm.subtitle: You do not need a long sit. Split the day — read, review, practice, listen — so the mind has time to file things away.
Rhythm.session1Body: Pick a short post. Read slowly and mark two or three unclear spots. Do not open a new word list in this session.
Rhythm.session2Title: Review only what you just met
Rhythm.session2Body: Say five words or two sentences from the morning. Speak them. Do not rewrite the whole page.
Rhythm.session3Body: Themed vocabulary, four sample sentences, one listening clip. When the time is up, stop — even if you want more.
Rhythm.session4Body: Replay audio you already know, look at the scene photos, retell in your own words. This session is for keeping, not stuffing.

Studio.title: Pictures of Linlin
Studio.subtitle: Three real moments on the page — a portrait, late light, and a trip.

Scenes.title: Learn from where you actually speak
Scenes.subtitle: Each topic is a photo corner and a few sentences you can use — café, market, travel, messages.
Scenes.scene1Body: Ask for a table, order a drink, request extra sugar. Short lines, spoken slowly, ready the next morning.
Scenes.scene2Body: Ask if something is left, bargain a little, take the bag. Learn stall by stall, not textbook chapter by chapter.
Scenes.scene3Body: Ask for directions, buy a ticket, say you are a little late. The sentences that save you in the middle of a street.
Scenes.scene4Body: Apologize for being late, set a time, send a pin. Practice the short written line — the rhythm of a real chat.

Tracks.title: What you will learn here
Tracks.subtitle: Four languages, one method: less theory, more examples, starting from sentences you use every day.
Tracks.viBody: Sounds, everyday vocabulary, and natural phrasing for beginners and foreigners.
Tracks.enBody: Linlin is learning English with you: useful sentences, collocations, and short listen-and-speak habits you can use immediately.
Tracks.zhBody: From having learned Chinese and taught it: pinyin, core characters, greetings, and daily situations — explained slowly and clearly.
Tracks.thBody: Linlin is learning Thai: consonants, vowels, tones, and phrases for travel, food, and first conversations.

Journal.post1Body: Why a short, regular session beats a long one you abandon.

Journal.post3Title: When you think you have no language talent
Journal.post3Body: Talent is often a habit kept long enough to feel natural.

Classroom.title: What a lesson looks like
Classroom.subtitle: About 15 minutes, with a clear goal, examples, and a short practice.
Classroom.item1Body: Eight to twelve words per lesson, tied to sample sentences — never a long list.
Classroom.item2Body: Greetings, directions, ordering food, messaging. Finish and speak.
Classroom.item3Body: Short audio at a kind speed, with a transcript you can check against.
Classroom.sampleBody: A 15-minute session: ten words tied to ordering, four sentences you can say at once, and one slow listening clip. You leave able to order a drink in the language you are learning.

Faq.title: Before you start
Faq.q1: Which language should a beginner choose?
Faq.a1: Choose the one you need first. If you are unsure, start with Vietnamese or English — those paths will have more lessons at the beginning.
Faq.a2: In this stage Linlin is opening the blog and foundation lessons. Content on the site is free to use.
Faq.q3: How long should I study each day?
Faq.a3: Fifteen minutes is enough. If you have extra time, read a blog post instead of adding more new words.
Faq.a4: She is not a school teacher. Vietnamese is home. She has studied Chinese and taught it. English and Thai she is learning now — lessons come from that real practice, everyday examples, and explanations that stay slow and clear.
Faq.q5: What if I skip a day?
Faq.a5: Nothing breaks. Come back with the smallest session: five minutes and two sentences. Do not try to make up the minutes — a steady rhythm matters more.
Faq.q6: Do I need to know the language already?
Faq.a6: No. Each scene starts from a greeting and a real situation. If you already know a little, use the review and slow-listening parts.
